Abstract

Omni-modal dialogue models can understand multimodal inputs and synthesize spoken replies, yet their responses remain visually disembodied. We introduce Ex-Omni-2D, an omni-modal dialogue framework that generates a coordinated response comprising text, personalized speech, and reference-conditioned video. Given a multimodal query, reference image, and reference audio, the model predicts a structured Visual Thought Plan (VTP) describing scene, emotion, and motion, followed by response text and native multi-codebook speech units. These units form a shared acoustictemporal interface: they are decoded into speech and aligned online with video frames. This interface enables the response and avatar pathways to be learned from heterogeneous speech, dialogue, and avatar-video data, avoiding the need for large-scale query–text–speech– video supervision. A full-sequence Video Generator serves as the primary Teacher. For efficient incremental generation, we further distill it into a few-step block-causal Streaming Student whose Prefix Streaming mechanism carries a clean latent across consecutive chunks to reduce cumulative late-chunk degradation. With four-step inference, the complete four-GPU pipeline achieves an end-to-end RTF of 1.293 at 400×720/720×400, providing a practical quality–efficiency operating point.
1 Introduction

Omni-modal dialogue systems increasingly understand speech, text, and visual inputs and answer with natural spoken replies (Xu et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025a,b; Xie and Wu, 2024a). Their responses, however, remain visually disembodied. We study omni-modal dialogue with dialoguenative video responses. Given a speech and/or text query, a reference image, and reference audio, the system generates an omni-modal response comprising response text, personalized speech, and a synchronized reference-conditioned video response. Here, dialogue-native describes the response-level interface: visual behavior is planned from the current dialogue and the acoustic-temporal condition is produced as part of the model’s own response process, rather than being specified manually or inferred only after a complete waveform has been rendered. Modality-specific generators still realize speech and video; this factorization is intentional and makes the response trainable from heterogeneous data.

Existing talking-avatar and audio-driven portrait animation methods provide strong visual synthesis (Peng et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Gan et al., 2025; Tu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b). Their visual component, however, is typically driven by a completed or externally supplied waveform and an optional manually prepared prompt, so it has no direct mechanism for deriving response-specific visual intent from the dialogue state. Joint audiovideo generation offers tighter modality coordination (Ruan et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a), yet generally creates content from prompts or reference signals rather than responding to a multimodal user query. What remains missing is a response framework that derives visual intent from dialogue and coordinates linguistic content, vocal realization, and visual behavior.

This setting motivates two modeling choices and one deployment requirement. First, recent speech-driven video generators often rely on a well-specified auxiliary text prompt, in addition to speech and a reference image, to control the scene, affect, and motion style (Gan et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025). In dialogue, manually designing this prompt or relying on a separate prompt-generation stage limits flexibility and can disconnect visual behavior from the current conversational state. Visual guidance should instead be inferred from the dialogue context and reference image. Second, directly mapping high-dimensional LLM states into a video generator is model-specific and costly, while fully omni-modal dialogue data pairing queries with response text, speech, and video are difficult to obtain at scale. A compact, temporally aligned interface is therefore needed to support speech synthesis, frame-aligned video conditioning, and staged learning from heterogeneous data. Finally, full-sequence video diffusion is too slow for interactive deployment, motivating an efficient streaming realization.

We introduce Ex-Omni-2D around these goals. The dialogue model first produces a structured Visual Thought Plan (VTP) describing scene, emotion, movement style, and motion details, followed by the user-facing response. It then generates native multi-codebook speech units as a shared acoustictemporal interface. The same units are decoded into personalized speech and aligned online with video frames, coupling vocal content and avatar motion without requiring a completed waveform. This factorization is motivated by data availability rather than by treating video as a post-hoc addon: speech and dialogue components learn from speech-centric supervision, whereas the avatar pathway learns from filtered video clips annotated with VTPs and teacher-forced speech units. At inference time, the dialogue-derived VTP and generated unit stream reconnect the separately supervised pathways. Thus, the framework obtains a coordinated response without assuming large-scale dialogue examples paired with target response videos.

The Video Generator has two realizations. A full-sequence Teacher provides the primary visual realization and is conditioned on reference appearance, VTP semantics, and frame-aligned speech units. For efficient deployment, we distill it into a few-step block-causal Streaming Student. We adopt AnyFlow’s flow-map and on-policy distillation objectives (Gu et al., 2026); our contribution is to integrate them with an avatar-specific streaming state and introduce Prefix Streaming. Each post-initial window carries one detached clean latent from the preceding chunk as a temporal prefix for three new latents, while maintaining chunkaligned speech conditioning. This design reduces cumulative late-chunk subject degradation without repeating output frames. The Student provides an efficiency-oriented alternative, while the Teacher remains preferred when visual quality is the primary objective.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks characterize dialogue, speech, video, audio–video synchronization, and efficiency performance. The fullsequence Teacher and incremental Student provide complementary quality- and efficiency-oriented operating points.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We formulate omni-modal dialogue with dialogue-native, reference-conditioned video responses and introduce a structured VTP that converts dialogue context into explicit visual guidance.

• We introduce a native multi-codebook speechunit interface for speech rendering, framealigned video conditioning, and pathwayspecific learning from heterogeneous speech, dialogue, and avatar-video data without fully paired video-response dialogues.

• We distill the full-sequence Teacher into a block-causal Streaming Student and introduce Prefix Streaming to reduce cumulative latechunk subject degradation while enabling efficient few-step incremental inference.
2 Related Work

Omni-modal Dialogue. Recent omni-modal large language models extend text-based interaction toward unified understanding and generation over speech, vision, and language. Representative systems explore speech-centered instruction following, real-time spoken response generation, crossmodal alignment, and unified multimodal generation within LLM-based architectures (Xie and Wu, 2024a,b; Luo et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; AI et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; Team, 2025). In parallel, speech language models further reduce the dependence on cascaded ASR–LLM–TTS pipelines by directly modeling spoken dialogue and speech generation (Ao et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Défossez et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024). However, most existing omni-modal dialogue systems still lack visual presence: they can understand speech and synthesize spoken responses, but do not directly generate a speaking visual agent.

Unified Audio-Video Generation. Aligned audio-video generation has been studied through both cascaded and joint paradigms. Audio-driven video synthesis first generates or receives a speech waveform and then animates a reference identity, which has led to strong progress in talking-head and human animation systems (Prajwal et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Gan et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025). The reverse direction, video-to-audio dubbing, generates sound or speech for a given silent video (Luo et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Sung-Bin et al., 2025). These conditional systems are effective visual or acoustic renderers, but their inputs usually do not include the conversational state from which response-specific visual behavior should be derived. Joint audio-video generation instead synthesizes both modalities within a unified or interacting generative process. More recent systems, including JavisDiT, Ovi, UniVerse-1, and UniAVGen, further explore large-scale or human-centric joint audio-video generation (Liu et al., 2026; Low et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026). UniVerse-1 stitches pre-trained audio and video experts to produce coordinated audio-video content, while UniAVGen introduces a dual-branch DiT with asymmetric cross-modal interactions and face-aware modulation for human-centric generation. These methods are the closest comparison group to our framework because they generate paired audio and video. Nevertheless, they are typically conditioned on prompts, speech content, reference audio, or reference images, rather than on a multimodal user query that requires response generation. Our contribution is not a new standalone renderer or a claim that all modalities share one generator. It is a dialogue-conditioned response formulation and a pair of explicit interfaces that allow semantic planning and acoustic timing to be produced within the response process, while modality-specific generators are trained with the supervision available to them.
3 Method

Ex-Omni-2D receives a multimodal user query $\boldsymbol { x } = \left( x _ { t } , x _ { s } \right)$ containing text, speech, or both, together with a reference image $I ^ { \mathrm { r e f } }$ and reference audio $a ^ { \mathrm { r e f } }$ . It generates an omni-modal response consisting of response text y, personalized speech, and a reference-conditioned video response V . As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework is organized around two intermediate interfaces. A structured Visual Thought Plan (VTP) p conveys high-level visual intent, while native multi-codebook speech units U provide the acoustic content and timing shared by speech and video generation. The dialogue model first emits the VTP and the user-facing response. Response-side hidden states then drive the Speech Generator, and the resulting units are decoded into a waveform and mapped to framealigned video conditions. The Video Generator has two realizations: a full-sequence Teacher generates the primary video response with bidirectional temporal context, while its deployment-oriented Prefix-Streaming Student renders the response incrementally while carrying temporal visual and motion state across chunks.

This interface uses all 16 codebooks while avoiding both completion-level waveform re-encoding and direct alignment from highdimensional LLM features. Its fixed temporal rate provides an explicit alignment to video frames, while its codec semantics preserve the information needed for speech rendering. It also decouples supervision: speech modeling can use speech and spoken-dialogue data, whereas the video pathway can use avatar clips with teacher-forced speech units. 3.4 Video Generator: Full-Sequence Teacher

3.5 Video Generator: Prefix-Streaming Student

The full-sequence Teacher remains the primary visual realization model, but its bidirectional, multistep denoising cannot emit video before the target clip is available. To provide the framework with an incremental deployment path, we distill it into a few-step block-causal Streaming Student. The Student prioritizes incremental generation and throughput; because it uses the same compact 1.3B backbone under a substantially reduced denoising budget, it is expected to trade visual fidelity for efficiency rather than supersede the Teacher. Following StreamAvatar (Sun et al., 2026), the Streaming Student uses bidirectional attention within each four-latent denoising window and causal attention across windows, allowing the current window to reuse cached reference and motion history without accessing future content. We adapt AnyFlow’s dual-time flow maps and on-policy distributionmatching objectives (Gu et al., 2026), while introducing our own avatar-specific streaming state and Prefix Streaming mechanism to align the referenceimage condition, generated speech, and clean motion history throughout distillation. The persistent state is designed for long-horizon avatar stability. The clean reference latent remains at the beginning of the sequence as a persistent reference anchor and is paired with a silent acoustic condition. Generated speech units are then aligned with their corresponding video chunks. Prefix Streaming keeps every DiT window at four latent slots. The initial window contains the reference latent and three newly generated latents. For every later window, the last clean latent of the preceding chunk is detached and reused as a one-latent prefix, followed by three new latent slots:

where sg denotes stop-gradient. The aligned acoustic condition follows the same overlap rule, and the clean prefix is re-injected before every denoising transition so that it cannot drift with the newly generated slots.

Our earlier no-prefix variant generated each later three-latent chunk directly from noise and relied only on the causal key–value cache for cross-chunk context. This cached history provides a useful global context, but it does not impose an explicit latent-space boundary condition on the first newly generated frame. Small boundary errors can therefore accumulate during autoregressive streaming:

early chunks may remain plausible, while later chunks increasingly drift or deform. Prefix Streaming addresses this failure mode by exposing the preceding terminal latent directly inside the current bidirectional denoising window. The shared clean latent anchors both sides of every chunk boundary, while stop-gradient and overlap-deduplicated cache updates prevent the anchor from being regenerated or counted twice.

Intermediate denoising forwards may read the persistent state but never write noisy keys and values into it. Only the completed clean chunk updates the cache; duplicate prefix positions are removed, so each later window advances the stream by exactly three new latent positions. This clean-only update prevents transient noise from contaminating later chunks. Detailed noise construction, temporal indexing, and cache updates are provided in Appendix L.2.1.
Once the VTP is complete, text and speech are generated incrementally. Every six acoustic frames, corresponding to 0.48 seconds at 12.5 Hz, trigger 12 video frames at 25 FPS:

The final incomplete speech block is padded only for computation and cropped to its valid duration. In parallel, a stateful multi-codebook decoder renders the same six units into a 0.48-second waveform segment using bounded left context. The reference latent in the initial window and the repeated prefix latent in later windows are internal conditions: neither is emitted again or decoded as a repeated output frame. Thus, each complete block still exposes exactly 12 new video frames and a synchronized speech segment derived from the same six units, without waiting for either modality to complete. The rate-aligned chunk construction is detailed in Appendix L.2.2.
3.6 Training Objectives and Stages

The core Ex-Omni-2D framework uses three pathway-specific supervision signals: an autoregressive language loss over the VTP and response protocol, a multi-codebook speech-generation loss conditioned on the response span, and a flowmatching video loss conditioned on the reference image, teacher-forced speech units, and VTP. These losses are enabled only when the corresponding supervision is available; they are not evaluated jointly on a fully paired query–text–speech–video dialogue sample. The common VTP schema and speech-unit representation provide the semantic and temporal contract between the response and avatar pathways. For efficient incremental deployment, the frozen Teacher then supervises the Streaming Student through the flow-map and onpolicy distribution-matching procedure described in Section 3.5; implementation details are provided in Appendix L.

Training uses three core stages followed by one deployment-oriented distillation stage. Stage 1: Speech Interface Alignment uses approximately 800K ASR and 1M TTS examples to train the Speech Projector and Speech Generator while keeping the LLM frozen. Stage 2: Omni-modal Response Adaptation updates the LLM, Speech Projector, and Speech Generator with InstructS2S-200K (Fang et al., 2025a) and OmniCharacter (Zhang et al., 2025a), introducing the structured VTP–response protocol and adapting the shared speech interface to interactive responses. Stage 3: Avatar Video Realization operates on about 140K filtered SpeakerVid clips. Each clip is converted into an avatar-response record containing a reference frame, a five-field VTP annotation, aligned multi-codebook speech units, and the target video. These records are not treated as query–response dialogue data; instead, they train the full-sequence Video Generator to realize the semantic and acoustic-temporal interfaces produced by the response pathway. The resulting model is frozen as the Teacher. Stage 4: Streaming Student Distillation then transfers the Teacher into the deployment-oriented Student through Phase I flow-map learning and Phase II on-policy distribution matching. This staged construction is central to the method: VTP and speech units reconnect the pathways at inference time without requiring large-scale dialogues paired with response videos. Data construction, optimization, and inference configurations are provided in Appendix L.
4 Experiments
4.1 Evaluation

Benchmarks and reference conditions. We conduct the audio-video evaluation on the CommonEval question-answering test set from VoiceBench (Chen et al., 2024a), which contains 200 speech queries. Because Ex-Omni-2D requires a reference image and reference audio, we sample paired reference conditions from the held-out

SpeakerVid test split (Zhang et al., 2025b). For each CommonEval query, the reference image and reference speech are held fixed across all compared methods; a baseline consumes only the modalities supported by its interface. For spoken question answering, we use AlpacaEval, CommonEval, and BBH from VoiceBench. For multi-turn dialogue quality, we use the 400-dialogue OmniCharacter benchmark (Zhang et al., 2025a) and follow its official CharacterEval protocol.

Metrics. We evaluate audio-video generation in terms of audio quality, video quality, and A-V Sync. For audio quality, we report Production Quality (PQ) and Content Usefulness (CU) from AudioBox (Tjandra et al., 2025), together with speaker similarity (SIM) under the Seed-TTS evaluation protocol (Anastassiou et al., 2024). For video quality, we report Subject Consistency (SC), Imaging Quality (IQ), and Dynamic Degree (DD) from VBench (Huang et al., 2024). DD is a descriptive measure of substantial motion rather than a monotonic measure of motion naturalness or semantic correctness. For A-V Sync, we report SyncNet confidence (Sync-C; higher is better), which measures lip-speech synchronization. Spoken question answering is scored using the open-source VoiceBench evaluation code. For OmniCharacter, we report all twelve official dimensions and their unweighted average, while highlighting Fluency, Coherency, and Consistency as the conversationalability metrics. Arrows indicate metrics with a preferred direction. Detailed metric definitions and scoring protocols are provided in Appendix A.

Comparison protocol. To control upstream response capacity, all cascaded baselines use Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Xu et al., 2025) as the common response controller, whose parameter scale is close to our 8B LLM backbone. A2V renderers receive speech from this controller, so PQ and CU are not attributed to the downstream renderer; SIM is reported only when the evaluated interface supports reference speech. UniAVGen’s main video metrics use A2V mode because its joint A-V mode supports only 5-second outputs, while its SIM score is obtained separately in RAVG reference-speech mode. All Ex-Omni-2D rows share the same generated speech and therefore have identical audio metrics. Because the compared paradigms expose different interfaces, Table 1 evaluates practical capability under each supported interface. Appendix Table 14 separately diagnoses the effect of changing the upstream response source while keeping each downstream renderer fixed.

text: 4.2 Audio-Video Comparison Results

Table 1 compares video generation, joint videoaudio generation, and dialogue-based omni-modal response generation under the protocol above. Among the downstream baselines, echomimic obtains the highest subject consistency (SC 97.87) and largest DD (74.00), UniAVGen obtains the highest imaging quality (IQ 68.02), and OmniAvatar-1.3B obtains the strongest synchronization (Sync-C 5.64). The Ex-Omni-2D Teacher does not dominate these standalone rendering metrics; instead, it obtains SIM 0.417, DD 72.00, and Sync-C 4.95 while additionally generating the dialogue response, personalized speech, and queryderived visual plan. Increasing the Streaming Student’s denoising budget from two to eight steps consistently increases SC, IQ, motion incidence, and Sync-C, exposing a controllable quality–efficiency trade-off. Appendix D analyzes this trade-off in detail, while Appendix Table 14 studies the effect of replacing the cascaded baselines’ upstream controller with Ex-Omni-2D.
4.3 Multi-turn Dialogue Quality

We use OmniCharacter (Zhang et al., 2025a) primarily to evaluate multi-turn dialogue quality: whether the model remains fluent, coherent, and consistent when responding with access to the preceding conversation. Following the benchmark’s complete official protocol, Table 2 also includes its character-consistency and role-playingattractiveness dimensions. Ex-Omni-2D obtains the highest reported Fluency, Coherency, and Consistency values among the compared methods, averaging 3.938 across the three metrics compared with 3.537 for its Qwen3-8B backbone. Its twelvedimension average is 3.283, close to Qwen3-8B at 3.264; we do not interpret this small overall difference as evidence of a uniform gain. The metricwise results include both increases and decreases relative to Qwen3-8B, revealing a capability tradeoff rather than across-the-board improvement. Appendix Table 9 directly evaluates the effect of providing dialogue history.
4.4 Speech QA Comparison Results

As shown in Table 3, on VoiceBench (Chen et al., 2024a), Ex-Omni-2D obtains 4.28 on AlpacaEval, 3.71 on CommonEval, and 58.70 on BBH. Within the listed systems, these are the second-highest reported scores after Qwen2.5-Omni. Appendix B separately reports the backbone and VTP ablations, including the measured language-capability tradeoff introduced by VTP generation.
4.5 Quality–Efficiency Trade-off

Table 4 summarizes the central quality–efficiency trade-off on the four-GPU pipeline. Each GPU has 16,896 CUDA cores, 132 streaming multiprocessors, and 141 GB of memory. The full-sequence Teacher uses 50 denoising steps and prioritizes visual quality. All Student operating points use the same validation-selected Prefix-Streaming checkpoint and differ only in whether two, four, or eight denoising steps are used at inference. RTF is measured relative to generated media duration, with values below 1 indicating faster-than-real-time generation. Quality metrics follow the CommonEval protocol in Table 1; throughput and E2E RTF use the equal-pixel $4 0 0 \times 7 2 0 / 7 2 0 \times 4 0 0$ settings. Here, streaming means that speech and video are emitted incrementally without waiting for the complete response; it does not imply that the full singlerequest pipeline is faster than real time. In the four-step pipeline, the first audible speech and first playable video chunk become available after 2.308 and 3.142 seconds, respectively. The complete event-level latency breakdown is reported in Appendix Table 12. The Teacher obtains the highest SC, IQ, DD, and Sync-C among our variants but is too slow for incremental use. The Student exposes three measured deployment points: two-step video inference reaches 39.5 FPS with the lowest quality metrics, whereas eight steps obtain higher IQ, DD, and Sync-C than the two- and four-step settings while retaining 15.6 FPS. The corresponding single-request E2E RTFs remain above 1, so these results establish incremental generation and fast video rendering rather than end-to-end real-time interaction. Figure 4 compares our earlier no-prefix Streaming Student with the Prefix-Streaming Student using both representative later-chunk examples and full-set temporal curves. In the examples, conditioning only through the causal cache produces visible facial or body degradation in later chunks, whereas the one-prefix-plus-three-new-latent design reduces these failures. Across all 200 CommonEval samples, Prefix Streaming changes SC from 92.85 to 93.65, IQ from 55.18 to 57.40, and Sync-C from 3.69 to 3.90, while both variants obtain the same DD of 32.00. We jointly ablate response-specific visual planning and personalized reference speech on the same 200 CommonEval requests, reference images, Teacher, and guidance scales as Table 1. To remove response-specific planning, we replace each generated plan with one fixed neutral five-field VTP. To remove personalized voice conditioning, we replace each matched reference utterance with one fixed public English utterance. Table 5 reports the complete 2 × 2 comparison. text: 5 Conclusion

We presented Ex-Omni-2D, an expressive omnimodal dialogue framework with dialogue-native video responses. Reference image and reference audio provide appearance and voice conditions, a structured Visual Thought Plan makes responsespecific visual intent explicit, and a native multicodebook speech space supports both speech rendering and frame-aligned avatar motion. The modality-specific realization pathways are trained separately because large-scale dialogues paired with target response videos are difficult to obtain; VTP and speech units reconnect them within the response process. The full-sequence Teacher provides the primary video realization, while the Prefix-Streaming Student transfers the same response interface into a few-step causal generator for incremental output. The two models expose complementary quality- and efficiency-oriented operating points.
Limitations

Although Ex-Omni-2D generates intelligible speech, its similarity to the reference speaker still leaves room for improvement. VTP provides highlevel semantic guidance rather than an independently sufficient video-control signal: the final realization is jointly conditioned on the plan and frame-aligned speech units, and a fixed balance between Text CFG and Audio CFG may not transfer uniformly across responses. Generating VTP in the shared autoregressive channel also introduces a measurable speech-QA and reasoning trade-off, motivating future planner isolation and adaptive cross-modal guidance. Our long-horizon analysis is limited to temporal subject stability and facialmotion regularity. The full-sequence Teacher remains computationally expensive because it uses bidirectional temporal context and a large denoising budget. The Streaming Student substantially improves video throughput and enables incremental generation, but it reports lower IQ, DD, and Sync-C than the Teacher under the evaluated settings. Moreover, its first playable video chunk arrives after 3.142 seconds and its single-request E2E RTF remains above 1 in our four-GPU pipeline, so streaming should be understood as incremental output rather than end-to-end real-time interaction. Scaling the causal video backbone, reducing response-planning latency, and improving few-step distillation may narrow these gaps. Accordingly, the Streaming Student is an efficiency-oriented deployment path rather than a replacement for the full-sequence Teacher.

text: A Evaluation Metric Details

Audio metrics. We use AudioBox-Aesthetics (Tjandra et al., 2025) to evaluate generated speech with PQ and CU. PQ focuses on perceptual production quality, reflecting whether the audio sounds clear, natural, stable, and free of obvious artifacts. CU evaluates the practical usefulness of the generated content, emphasizing intelligibility and semantic completeness. Compared with strict worderror-rate matching, CU better captures whether the generated speech is usable and understandable from a listener’s perspective. We additionally report SIM using the official Seed-TTS evaluation protocol: WavLM-Large (Chen et al., 2021) and an ECAPA-TDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020) speakerverification head embed the generated and reference speech, and SIM is their cosine similarity.

Video metrics. We use VBench (Huang et al., 2024) to evaluate generated videos with SC, IQ, and DD; none of these metrics requires a groundtruth video. SC measures the temporal consistency of the generated subject, IQ measures perceptual frame quality such as sharpness and visible artifacts, and DD uses optical-flow magnitude to report the proportion of videos with substantial motion.

A-V Sync. We use SyncNet confidence (Sync-C) (Chung and Zisserman, 2016; Prajwal et al., 2020) to evaluate whether mouth movements are temporally aligned with the generated speech. Sync-C measures the separation between the best audiovideo alignment and competing temporal offsets, so higher values indicate more confident synchronization.

Speech QA metrics. For spoken question answering, we use AlpacaEval (Li et al., 2023), CommonEval (Chen et al., 2024a), and BBH (Suzgun et al., 2022) from VoiceBench (Chen et al., 2024a) and follow the open-source VoiceBench evaluation code. AlpacaEval and CommonEval use GPT-4o-mini to judge open-ended response quality on a five-point scale, where 5 is the best score; AlpacaEval emphasizes general instruction following, whereas CommonEval focuses on common spoken QA. BBH evaluates complex QA requiring multistep reasoning, logical composition, and abstract thinking, and is reported as accuracy. Each BBH subtask then applies task-specific string matching or regular expressions to convert free-form responses into binary labels, such as yes/no answers, option choices, navigation decisions, truthfulness judgments, or sports-plausibility judgments. The final score is computed as the percentage of correct predictions.
B Additional Dialogue Capability Results

Effect of VTP supervision. We isolate the effect of training the LLM to emit the structured VTP before its user-facing response. As shown in Table 7, response-only training without VTP supervision obtains 3.82 on CommonEval and 61.10 on BBH. Adding VTP supervision changes these scores to 3.71 and 58.70, corresponding to decreases of 0.11 and 2.40 points, respectively. This is a measurable language-capability trade-off rather than a uniform preservation result: the shared autoregressive channel gains an explicit visual-planning interface at the cost of lower speech-QA and reasoning scores. Separating or parameter-isolating the planner may reduce this interference in future work.

L.1 Data Construction

ASR and TTS data. Our Stage-1 speech data contain about 800K ASR examples and 1M TTS examples. The ASR portion consists of roughly 300K examples from LibriSpeech (Panayotov et al., 2015) and 500K randomly sampled examples from Emilia (He et al., 2024). For TTS supervision, we randomly sample 1M text examples from Emilia and synthesize speech using Qwen3-TTS (Hu et al.,

2026). We use Qwen3-TTS because of its strong speech quality, which allows the Speech Generator to learn a usable speech-output capability from a relatively moderate amount of synthesized training data.

Dialogue data. For Stage-2 omni-modal response adaptation, we use examples from InstructS2S-200K (Fang et al., 2025a) and OmniCharacter (Zhang et al., 2025a). InstructS2S-200K provides speech-to-speech conversational supervision, while OmniCharacter contributes character-grounded, multi-turn dialogue examples. Together, they update the LLM, Speech Projector, and Speech Generator, adapting the structured VTP–response protocol and shared speech interface toward interactive and character-consistent responses.

Video generation data. For the avatarrealization pathway in Stage 3, we use SpeakerVid (Zhang et al., 2025b) as the source video dataset. We apply the automated filtering pipeline described below, obtaining about 140K training clips. For every retained clip, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) constructs a five-field VTP describing the first frame, scene, emotion, movement style, and motion details using the prompt in Appendix M. We then tokenize its aligned speech with the Qwen3-TTS Tokenizer (Hu et al., 2026) to obtain the native multi-codebook video condition. Each clip is therefore converted into an avatar-response record containing a reference image, VTP annotation, aligned speech units, and target video. We do not regard these records as dialogue data: they contain no paired user query and serve specifically to train the diffusion model to realize the VTP and speech-unit interfaces.

SpeakerVid Filtering and Record Construction. Audio segmentation first produces an aligned 16- kHz waveform and a 25-FPS video clip. We then apply the seven filters in Table 16. A clip is retained only if every check passes. This data-pipeline stage is distinct from the model-training stages in Section L.2. For each retained clip, we use the first frame as the appearance reference, annotate the five-field VTP with Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), and tokenize the aligned speech with the Qwen3-TTS Tokenizer (Hu et al., 2026). This produces 16 codebook streams at 12.5 Hz. The final diffusion record contains the target video, reference frame, VTP, and speech tokens. At 25 FPS, each speech-token frame aligns with exactly two video frames. This record construction supplies the conditions required by the avatar generator, but it does not create a paired dialogue-video example.

text: L.2 Framework Training and Student Distillation

Stage 1: Speech Interface Alignment. We first use approximately 800K ASR and 1M TTS examples to establish the bidirectional speech interface while freezing the LLM, Speech Encoder, and Vision Encoder. ASR batches update the Speech Projector, grounding speech inputs in the LLM representation space. TTS batches update the Qwen3- TTS-initialized (Hu et al., 2026) Speech Generator, teaching it to predict native multi-codebook units from response-side representations. Thus, Stage 1 updates the Speech Projector and Speech Generator, with each batch activating only the branch for which it provides supervision.

Stage 2: Omni-modal Response Adaptation. We then jointly update the LLM, Speech Projector, and Speech Generator using examples from InstructS2S-200K (Fang et al., 2025a) and OmniCharacter (Zhang et al., 2025a). The LLM learns the structured <thinking>–<response> protocol, where the thinking block contains the VTP, while speech supervision remains restricted to the response span. This stage adapts the aligned speech interface toward interactive and characterconsistent spoken replies without requiring a target response video.

Stage 3: Avatar Video Realization. Finally, we train the full-sequence avatar diffusion model on the 140K SpeakerVid-derived records described above. Each training example provides a reference image, an automatically annotated VTP, teacherforced multi-codebook speech units, and a target video. The diffusion model is therefore optimized to realize the same semantic and acoustictemporal interfaces that the response pathway produces at inference time. Importantly, this stage does not assume that the source clips are dialogue responses and does not introduce synthetic user queries merely to label them as dialogue data. The interface-based decomposition is what permits the response and video pathways to use their respective data sources: dialogue supervision teaches what to say and how to plan a response, whereas SpeakerVid supervision teaches how to render a supplied plan and speech-unit sequence as video.

Stage 4: Streaming Student Distillation. After Stage 3, the full-sequence Video Generator is frozen as the Teacher. Stage 4 trains the Streaming Student in two successive phases rather than treating them as separate framework stages. Phase I learns source–destination flow maps from the Teacher, and Phase II performs on-policy chunked Student rollouts with distribution matching while retaining the flow-map objective. This hierarchy keeps the three data-oriented training stages distinct from the deployment-oriented distillation procedure. The data sources and trainable modules of each stage are specified in the stage descriptions above and the implementation paragraph below. For the video pathway, Stage 3 uses 125-frame SpeakerVid clips assigned to three 720p aspectratio buckets, while both Stage 4 phases use 121- frame windows with the same buckets.

Optimization and implementation. We implement and train the framework with PyTorch 2.7.0 and CUDA 12.6. Table 17 summarizes the stagewise optimization settings and the two-phase Student distillation protocol; the corresponding data and trainable modules are specified in the stage descriptions above. Table 18 reports the inference configuration used for the main quality evaluation. Both models use empty negative prompts and deterministic dialogue-response decoding (temperature 0 and top-p 1), while all Student results use the same validation-selected Prefix-Streaming checkpoint and differ only in their denoising budgets.

Video clips are decoded at 25 FPS. We assign each clip to its nearest aspect-ratio bucket among 400×720, 720×400, and 720×720, resize isotropically, and center-crop to the exact bucket without padding. A random contiguous window of 125 frames is used for Teacher SFT and 121 frames for Streaming Student distillation; short clips repeat their final frame. Window starts are aligned to the 12.5-Hz speech-token grid. For CommonEval, each sample uses a fixed reference image taken from the first frame and its speaker-matched reference speech. Reference speech is converted to mono, resampled to 24 kHz for the Speech Generator, and deterministically cropped to 3–10 seconds using seed 42; query speech and video-conditioning audio are mono at 16 kHz. Teacher and Streaming Student quality comparisons reuse the same text response, VTP, speech units, waveform, reference image, and reference speech, so their reported differences isolate the video generator.

text: L.2.1 Prefix and Cache Implementation

For every post-initial window, the final prepared acoustic condition from chunk m − 1 prefixes the three new conditions for chunk m. To preserve the training-time random-number trajectory, noise is sampled for all four latent slots before the fixed prefix slot is overwritten. The clean prefix is then re-injected before every denoising transition. Each chunk is mapped from noise to a clean latent estimate through the learned transitions. Intermediate denoising forwards may read the persistent state but do not write noisy keys and values into it. After the final transition, an additional identity-map forward with $t = r = 0$ encodes only the completed clean chunk into the cache:

For a post-initial window, temporal positions begin at the current global offset minus one. The duplicate prefix position is removed from the historical keys and values before attention, and the clean-cache pass appends only the three new latent positions. Consequently, the global offset advances by three rather than four, no temporal position is duplicated, and transient noisy features never enter the persistent history. Each output chunk therefore uses the configured denoising transitions followed by one clean-cache encoding forward.
L.2.2 Rate-Aligned Streaming Chunks

The speech interface emits one multi-codebook acoustic frame every $1 / 1 2 . 5 ~ = ~ 0 . 0 8$ seconds, whereas the avatar pathway decodes video at 25 FPS. Each acoustic frame therefore aligns exactly with two output video frames. We group six acoustic frames into one streaming block, giving <sup>6</sup>12.5 12 = 0.48 s. Thus, every speech block maps to exactly 12 decoded video frames; under the video VAE, these correspond to the three new latent frames produced by each causal block. Internally, each post-initial DiT window prepends the preceding block’s final clean latent and prepared acoustic condition, yielding one overlap prefix plus three new latents. The overlap is excluded from VAE emission and external output, so the public stream still advances by exactly 12 frames. This construction keeps acoustic units, waveform segments, decoded video frames, latent blocks, and cache updates on integer temporal boundaries. The final partial block is padded only for batched computation, after which both waveform and video outputs are cropped to their valid duration. We use the same block definition during Student post-training and streaming inference.
